phonemes.desc: Short alpha with acute pitch — the name shouts, a battle cry compressed into one syllable.
Rho plus long eta and sigma — the long vowel sustains the shout into a name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-rays' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched high, like a command to charge.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἀρά (ará), 'ruin, bane' — the traditional Greek derivation (LSJ); the god is the calamity he brings

pronunciation.note: Árēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἄρης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name sounds like a wound being named: short, sharp, and final.

domains.title: The Bane of Men
domains.subtitle: War, Battle Fury, and Courage
domains.lead: Árēs is the god of war unprocessed — the killing rage, the blood-price, the panic on the field. The Greeks honored him and plainly feared him, but their literature is frank: raw violence without judgment is the most easily defeated force on Olympus.

cards.name: Battle Fury
cards.desc: The bloodlust that makes warriors forget fear and reason alike.

cards.name: Courage and Terror
cards.desc: He fills both sides with courage; to fight is to breathe his presence.

cards.name: Defeat and Wounding
cards.desc: Unlike Athena, Árēs is often wounded and driven from the field — war is not always victorious.

cards.name: The Lover of Aphrodítē
cards.desc: His affair with Aphrodítē makes war the counterpart of desire; their union produces Harmonia.

symbols.name: Spear
symbols.meaning: His constant attribute in art and epic; with it he strides the field at Troy, and with it Diomedes wounds him in Iliad 5.

symbols.name: Helmet
symbols.meaning: The crested bronze casque; on the Ares Borghese (Louvre) he lounges in helmet and shield — war at rest.

symbols.name: Shield
symbols.meaning: The hoplite's aspis; Homer marks his status by giving him attendants to carry his war-gear.

symbols.name: Vulture
symbols.meaning: The battlefield scavenger; in the Iliad's vulture-similes its arrival is the war's signature sound.

symbols.name: Burning torch
symbols.meaning: The brand of the sack — war as fire, the element the Iliad has Árēs breathe around the field.

symbols.name: Dog
symbols.meaning: The corpse-eater; the Iliad's 'dogs and birds' formula (1.4–5) distributes his harvest between the two scavengers.

mythology.lead: Árēs is the only major Olympian whom the other gods routinely humiliate. His myths share one thesis: war without wisdom is self-defeating. Beaten by mortals, trapped by craftsmen, and tried in a murder court, the war god survives as the Greeks' most honest portrait of violence — and even Zeús calls him hateful.

myths.title: Struck by Diomedes
myths.text: The Iliad gives the war god his definitive humiliation in Book 5 (855–909). Fighting for the Trojans, Árēs encounters the Greek Diomedes, into whom Athēnâ has poured strength and, most insulting, clear sight — the vision that lets a mortal look straight at gods. Guided by her hand, Diomedes hurls his spear into Árēs’s belly; the god roars with the voice of nine thousand warriors or ten thousand, a black cloud of pain gathers around him, and he flees to Olympus, where he collapses and wails like a woman. Zeús is unmoved: of all the Olympians, he says, Árēs is most hateful — a god of strife, war, and slaughter who delights only in ruin. The scene is the Iliad’s thesis in miniature. Discipline, strategy, and divine counsel defeat fury every time — and even fury’s own father will not speak for it.

myths.title: Caught with Aphrodítē
myths.text: In the song of Demodocus (Odyssey 8.266–366), Hēphaistos discovers his wife Aphrodítē in bed with Árēs — because the all-seeing Hēlios tells him. The smith rigs invisible bonds, ‘fine as spiders’ webs, of forged adamant,’ over the bed, pretends to leave for Lemnos, and catches the lovers mid-embrace. He calls the gods to witness, and the immortals gather to laugh: Hermês admits he would trade places with Árēs even in triple chains; only the goddesses stay home out of modesty. Eventually Poseidôn guarantees the adulterers’ compensation, the net is loosed, and the two flee — Árēs to Thrace, Aphrodítē to Cyprus. The story is the Greeks’ comic masterpiece of theodicy, but its edge is real: the god of war, stripped of armor and allies, is merely ridiculous. War in the bedroom is not war at all.

myths.title: The First Murder Trial on the Areopagus
myths.text: A genuinely archaic myth makes Árēs the defendant in history’s first murder trial. Poseidôn’s son Halirrhothius raped Árēs’s daughter Alkippe; Árēs killed him on the spot and was charged by the sea-god before the assembled gods. The court convened on the rocky hill west of the Athenian Acropolis, and the twelve gods, judging the killing a just defense, acquitted him (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.2; Euripides, Electra 1258–1263). From the trial of Árēs — Areios Pagos, the ‘Hill of Ares’ — Athens’ most solemn court took its name, the Areopagus, which long judged homicide and impiety and would, in St Paul’s day, examine the apostle himself. The myth is remarkable for what it admits: even the personification of killing must answer to a court. Greek war, unlike its god, lived under law.

myths.title: Kadmos Serves an Eternal Year
myths.text: When Kadmos came seeking his sister Europa, a cow led him to a spring near what became Thebes — a spring guarded by a dragon called a son of Árēs (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.4.1–2). The dragon killed Kadmos’s men for daring to draw water; Kadmos killed the dragon and, on Athēnâ’s advice, sowed its teeth in the plain. Armed men, the Spartoi, sprang up and fell upon one another until five remained — ancestors of the Theban nobility. For shedding the dragon’s blood Kadmos owed Árēs a penalty: he served the god for ‘an eternal year’ — the ancient scholiasts explain the phrase as eight years — and was then given Harmonia, Árēs’s own daughter, as his bride. The story binds the city’s founding to the war god and shows his signature logic: bloodshed generates warriors, penalty generates marriage, and war fathers the very houses it later destroys.

myths.title: Terror, Rout, and Harmony
myths.text: Hesiod’s Theogony (933–937) catalogues what war produces when it lies with love. By Aphrodítē, Árēs fathers Harmonia — concord, the settlement after conflict; by himself he fathers Deimos and Phobos, Terror and Rout, his chariot companions, and on the shield of Achilles (Iliad 18.535–540) Eris and Kydoimos walk the field with black Ker, dragging away the wounded and the dead. The genealogy is economical to the point of bleakness: every battle has exactly four products — the terror before it, the rout within it, the strife that starts it, and, if it ever ends, the fragile harmony after. The Greeks refused to let war be pure. Even their war god is married to the goddess of love, and even his most terrible children share his house with agreement itself.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Árēs with Mars, but the equation was imperfect. Mars was an agricultural as well as military god, far more central to Roman state religion than Árēs ever was to Greek civic life. The Roman March (Martius) and Tuesday in Romance languages preserve his name. In later European art, Mars became one of the seven planets and a standard allegory of war. The contrast between Greek contempt for Árēs and Roman reverence for Mars reveals how differently the two cultures understood organized violence.
lore.culturalLegacy: Árēs is the god we prefer not to invoke. Modern culture usually portrays him as a villain or a brute, while Athena gets the credit for strategic warfare. Yet his honesty is valuable: he represents war as it actually is — chaotic, bloody, and often stupid. The Spartans, who worshipped him more than other Greeks, understood that courage is a virtue even when wisdom is absent. In an age of permanent conflict, Árēs reminds us that not all wars are just, and that the god of battle is not the god of victory.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Árēs is the god of violence without justification. He does not defend cities like Athēnâ; he simply fights, and the Iliad never once praises him. The Greeks were clear-eyed about him because they understood that war is sometimes necessary but never noble in itself. A soldier needs courage; a general needs judgment. Árēs supplies only the first, and Zeús calls him hateful for it.

Modern culture prefers its war gods subtle or invisible. Árēs refuses subtlety. The restoration of his name — short, pitched, and final — declines to sanitize the ancient world’s most honest admission: that the appetite for war is divine, eternal, and very often stupid.
lore.archaeology: The temple of Ares in the Athenian Agora, excavated by the American School, is a Roman-period reassembly of a Classical temple probably moved from Acharnae. Pausanias records sanctuaries of Ares at Geronthrae in Laconia and at Thebes. Thrace yielded weapons and horse-gear dedications to a martial deity identified with Ares. The Ares Borghese type (Louvre), once thought an Ares by Scopas, preserves his bearded, helmeted image in Roman marble.
